flashcards.q: How many network round trips does a fully cold DNS lookup take, worst case vs common case?
flashcards.a: Worst case up to 3-4 (root, TLD, authoritative), each a separate round trip. Common case is 1 round trip to the authoritative server, since root and TLD delegation are usually already cached (TTLs of days).

flashcards.q: Why is DNS-based failover often much slower than the configured TTL suggests?
flashcards.a: TTL is advisory, not enforced -- OS resolvers, app-runtime caches, and corporate/ISP resolvers routinely cache longer than instructed or override TTL entirely. Real propagation can take minutes to hours despite a 60s TTL.

flashcards.q: Why can't a CNAME sit at a domain's zone apex?
flashcards.a: The apex must also hold NS (and typically SOA) records for zone delegation, and DNS disallows any other record type coexisting at a name that has a CNAME. The workaround is a provider-specific ALIAS/ANAME record that resolves like a CNAME but is flattened to an A record at the edge.

flashcards.q: What's the mechanical difference between L4 and L7 load balancing?
flashcards.a: L4 (e.g. AWS NLB) routes on IP/TCP headers only -- no HTTP parsing, near-zero added latency, can't route on path/host. L7 (e.g. AWS ALB, Envoy) terminates TLS and parses HTTP, enabling path/host/header/cookie routing at the cost of real per-request CPU.

flashcards.q: Why does consistent hashing matter for a distributed cache?
flashcards.a: Naive hash(key) % n remaps nearly every key when n changes (a node joins/leaves), wiping the cache. Consistent hashing places keys and servers on a ring so a node change remaps only ~1/n of keys, leaving the rest warm.

flashcards.q: Why use virtual nodes (~100-200 per physical node) in a consistent hash ring?
flashcards.a: A single ring position per physical node produces uneven arc sizes by chance. Multiple virtual positions per physical node smooth the key distribution close to uniform.

flashcards.q: What's the thundering-herd risk of an aggressive health check interval?
flashcards.a: A short interval with a low failure threshold can eject a large fraction of the fleet simultaneously during a correlated blip (shared dependency hiccup, GC pause across the fleet), dumping all traffic onto survivors and cascading. Fix: require N consecutive failures, stagger checks, cap max-ejection %.

flashcards.q: Why do sticky sessions fight horizontal scaling?
flashcards.a: They pin a client to a specific backend instance, so you can't freely add/remove instances without disrupting pinned sessions, and rolling deploys must drain sticky connections rather than just cycling instances. IP-hash affinity additionally hot-spots when many clients share one NAT IP.

flashcards.q: Does anycast route to the physically nearest server?
flashcards.a: No. The same IP is announced from multiple sites via BGP, and routers pick the path with the best BGP cost (shortest AS-path, policy attributes) -- often correlated with distance but not the same thing. A client can be routed to a farther site with better peering.

flashcards.q: Why is anycast/BGP failover faster than DNS-based failover?
flashcards.a: BGP convergence after withdrawing an announcement is typically seconds. DNS failover depends on clients/resolvers honoring TTL, which they routinely don't -- real propagation can take minutes to hours.

flashcards.q: What is CDN origin shielding and what failure does it prevent?
flashcards.a: Designating one CDN PoP as the sole one allowed to fetch from origin on a miss; other PoPs fetch from the shield. Prevents the thundering herd where a popular object's TTL expires and dozens of edge PoPs simultaneously hit origin at once.

flashcards.q: What CDN cache-key mistake causes a personalization data leak, not just poor hit rate?
flashcards.a: Caching a personalized/auth-dependent response at a shared cache layer without Cache-Control: private -- another user can be served the first user's cached response, which is a security incident, not just a performance bug.

flashcards.q: Why is negative DNS caching (NXDOMAIN) important to know about?
flashcards.a: NXDOMAIN/NODATA answers are cached too, per the zone's SOA negative-cache TTL (commonly minutes to an hour). Querying a name before its record propagates can get you a cached 'doesn't exist' answer that outlives the record's actual creation.
